beta_new: Route climbs class 2-3 scrambling to a class 4 chimney, then traverses class 3 ledges on the southeast face. Final pitch involves friction slab climbing (class 5.6) or alternate cracks left of the slab. Route-finding to the crux can be challenging. The summit horn is extremely exposed with only room for one person at a time; rope belays required for final exposed sections.

moves.from: The south face is accessed from Spire Col at 7,760 feet.
Descent via two 60-meter rappels to scree.

beta_new: Pitch 1 climbs face moves protected by 3 bolts above a left-trending overlap (5.10a); pitch 2 climbs past two bolts to a crack (5.10a) with a traverse right at the third bolt; pitch 3 is a sport-style pitch with a hard start (5.10a) easing into 5.7-5.8 face climbing; pitch 4 finishes on fun 5.6-5.7 cracks.

Fully bolted 100 ft (30 m) sport pitch rated 5.10b/c. The FA party (Wylie Moreshead) recommends starting left of the bolt line and straddling the low nose feature cheval-style rather than pulling straight onto it, keeping the rope managed on the inside leg to avoid an awkward twist. 12 bolts lead to chains at the top.

moves.from: 12 bolts lead to chains at the top.
12 bolts lead to chains at the top.

beta_new: Route-finding requires staying on the correct gully (right-side route preferred over left). Traverse a ledge across the backside of the southern tower with Class 3-4 moves and occasional exposure. Navigate a slight overhang with a squeeze-through section (Class 3), then traverse the summit tower's backside to a small spur. Final approach involves either climbing a 15-foot Class 4 solid face or wrapping around the left side on Class 3 blocks to reach the summit register.

moves.from: Approach the peak from Park Creek campground by ascending a loose talus slope, bearing left toward a cirque below the towers.
Slings are in place near the summit for rappel anchors.

beta_new: P1 follows bolts at 5.10 to chains, then trends left past additional anchor sets. The next section is a corner with traditional gear and a slab. The standout crux pitch is bolted with small trad gear, trending up-right through corners and over a roof (5.11c) to an anchor, after which easier 5.10 slabby climbing leads to the top of the cliff.

Roughly 2,000 vertical feet of water and alpine ice: a lower ramp of about 600 ft of WI2-3 water ice, then a first snowfield, a second snowfield, and an AI2 exit step to reach the upper mountain. The FA party found excellent neve and abundant ice but only carried two titanium ice screws, supplementing protection with knifeblade pitons in compact rock between ice sections. Because the line only forms briefly, it has almost no repeat trip-report history and is considered one of the Cascades' 'forgotten' ice testpieces.

From a high camp near Vista Lakes or Summit Chief Lake, parties traverse off-trail north across Vista Ridge to Summit Chief Pass and into the peak's southeast basin. Snowfields below the southeast face are climbed via a snow finger to gain the south ridge (the first, left-most finger dead-ends at a notch, requiring a rightward traverse to the upper snowfield corner). From the ridge notch, Class 2-3 (locally Class 4) scrambling on loose, convoluted sandstone/siltstone slabs, gullies and a short exposed ramp leads to the summit.

Ascend broken rock and ledges (loose throughout) toward the summit ridge; route-finding is the crux — at least one spot appears to cliff out but a cairned Class 3 crack around the corner allows passage. Continue Class 3 scrambling to the summit.

moves.from: From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, hike the Royal Creek/Upper Dungeness Trail through Royal Basin, continue past Royal Lake into Upper Royal Basin, then leave the maintained trail and travel cross-country to the base of Sundial's east/northeast face.

beta_new: Starts with an approach pitch of rambly ice leading to a solid ~25 ft near-vertical curtain (WI4), continues up nearly 60m of solid fat WI3 ice in the main gully, eases through 100+m of easier terrain with ice smears through an easy chimney, then finishes with a short WI3 step before the upper snowfields.

Most ascents happen mid-traverse on the Northern Pickets high route (Luna–East Fury–West Fury–Swiss–Spectre Plateau–Phantom–Ghost–Challenger), first strung together as a continuous crest traverse by Wayne Wallace and Josh Kaplan in 2005 (VI 5.7 overall for the traverse, though Swiss itself is comparatively easy 3rd/4th-class terrain). From a camp near West Fury, cross a short glacier/permanent snowfield northwest of West Fury to the Swiss–Fury saddle, then climb the southwest face on notably solid rock (a welcome break from the loose ground nearby) to the summit ridge, descending near the northwest ridge to continue toward Spectre Plateau/Phantom Peak. A separate party approaching from the south (as part of a Mystery Ridge/Northern Pickets enchainment) climbed Swiss's south side directly from a camp at Pickell Pass: straightforward class 3 rock with some ridge-walking needed to identify the true high point, about 2.5 hours round trip. A reliable spring/running water source below the southwest snowfield is a notable resource on an otherwise dry crest.

Most parties backpack in and camp at Cooney or Martin Lakes rather than attempting the roughly 18-20 mile round trip in a single push. From Cooney Lake, a boot path continues about a mile to gain the broad Southeast Ridge, which is class 1-2 for almost its entire length; only the last few hundred feet below the summit require actual hands-on scrambling over large, mostly stable boulders, with a few exposed class 3 moves right at the top. The peak is frequently linked with Martin Peak via an easy, open class 1-2 ridge walk to the north, forming part of the popular 'Sawtooth Slam' traverse with Mount Bigelow.

An alternate to the Southeast Ridge standard route: from the Boiling Lake area, a way trail contours below Martin and Switchback Peaks at roughly 7,200-7,300 ft; from there, climbers either pick up a boot path up the west face or climb the west ridge proper (class 2-3) to the summit. It sees far less traffic than the Cooney Lake/Southeast Ridge approach and is more commonly used by parties already in the Boiling Lake/Martin Peak basin as part of a larger Sawtooth Ridge traverse.

From the Artist Point parking lot (about 5,075 ft), the Table Mountain Trail climbs a series of tight, exposed switchbacks cut into the mountain's southeast-facing rock face for roughly half a mile and about 400 ft of gain to reach the broad summit plateau. Beyond the switchbacks the trail is gentle, crossing the plateau to tarns with Shuksan views around the 1.3-mile mark; most hikers turn around there. The trail continues west and eventually drops to link with the Chain Lakes Trail system. The route is entirely above treeline, narrow and cliff-edge in its lower half, and not recommended for those uneasy with exposure or for small children; dogs are not allowed.

From Tailgunner Pass, scramble up Tailgunner's west ridge and south-facing scree/rock slopes to the summit dome; a narrow summit ledge is the crux and can be exposed or icy if snow lingers. In late-spring snow conditions parties have instead cramponed up a north-slope snow route and surmounted a corniced west-ridge headwall — a more technical, roped variation not represented by the Class 3 rating.

moves.from: From Barclay Lake Trailhead, walk a quarter mile back down the road to a spur road, cross Barclay Creek and climb the Tailgunner Creek drainage/couloir to Tailgunner Pass (~5,320 ft), a broad saddle between Gunn Peak's ridge and Tailgunner.

beta_new: Climb the roughly 1,200-ft, up-to-35-degree couloir (crampons and ice axe, or ski crampons for splitboard/ski parties), then scramble to the NW Ridge where one 5.4 rock pitch leads to the summit.

moves.from: Approach via the Honeycomb Glacier — either descending from a high camp on Kololo Peaks or traversing in from the White River side over the PCT/Whitechuck and Suiattle Glaciers — to a col west of Tenpeak, then cross onto the Honeycomb Glacier and traverse to the couloir's base.

beta_new: From Thunder Basin at 5,180 feet, ascend snowfields and rocky slopes toward the summit block. The final two pitches involve Class 4 scrambling up a gully left of the summit col (approximately 85 feet to a ledge), followed by a longer pitch up a face toward a broken chimney containing a good jam crack that leads directly to the summit. Crampons and ice axe essential for snowfield sections. The route sees minimal traffic and requires solid route-finding skills.

moves.from: A fixed pin exists for rappel descent assistance.
moves.evidence: wenatcheeoutdoors.org 2016 Tenpeak (fixed pin ~50 ft from summit, north corner, used for descent); cascadeclimbers.com topic 3330 (rappel piton on the N corner, as in Beckey).
moves.value: A fixed pin about 50 ft below the summit, on its north corner, is often used for the descent.

beta_new: A long, mostly non-technical mountaineering route that is more of a route-finding and stamina challenge than a climbing one. From the base-camp area near the forks of Lena Creek, climbers' paths lead up the creek drainage to a broad avalanche slope/meadow below the first cliff band; cross this and enter the couloir (snow- or rock-filled depending on season), following it up through the narrow "Hourglass" constriction near ~5,800 ft. Above the Hourglass the couloir broadens; work up and right, staying on firmer rock, then trend back left/up through loose scree to the summit. Early/mid-season the couloir holds continuous snow (ice axe and crampons required, with snow up to 40-45 degrees); by late summer it is a loose, snow-free scree-and-rock scramble.

moves.from: From the Lena Lake Trailhead, hike past Lena Lake and through the Valley of the Silent Men to a base-camp area near where the trail meets Lena Creek's forks.

beta_new: Fourth-class scrambling leads to a notch near 6,100 ft and a descent on steep snow into the Great Basin, below the North Brother. From there the traverse is 7 roped pitches (statically belayed, though simulclimbing is possible): moderate snow pitches on the east ridge, a sparsely protected rock traverse on the west side, mixed rock-and-snow sections with moat belays, and a final steep couloir ascent to the South Brother summit. The route is recommended north-to-south.

Starts on the north side of the tower, about 50 feet below the notch, at two semi-parallel diagonal cracks that form the crux. After the diagonals, the route follows a flake past a dead tree to a belay tree (reportedly deteriorating — back it up with gear). Pitch 2 traverses left beneath an overhang to a corner, then continues about 20 feet to the mouth of a cave, which is climbed through (~20 feet) to a belay on the far side. Pitch 3 climbs an easier crack and face to a tree belay at the summit.

From the high camp, traverse beneath the steep east face to the southeast side of the peak, where a hidden gully gives easy access to the face. Climb a chimney about 200 ft high, then a slabby face. Below the summit slab there are a few harder moves where the route mixes face and ridge climbing, with some scrubby vegetation. Allow about three hours from timberline. Because the Pickets guard several summits from a shared basin, parties often combine this peak with Mount Degenhardt, Mount Terror, or Inspiration Peak on the same trip.

Fred Beckey reportedly attempted this face earlier and found it traumatic enough to never return, and it came to be regarded as a last great problem perhaps best left unclimbed. Layton and Wolfe finally forced a route in 2005 after a brutal approach, climbing banded gneiss that offered very little solid protection; every hold reportedly required testing, and pitons often wouldn't set. Note: the grade/length is variously given as V+ 5.9+ A2- and ~2,500 ft, and as V+ 5.11- and 2,400 ft — the latter figures are used here, but treat the discrepancy as a sign of how approximate any grade is on this kind of loose, unrepeated wall.

Pitch 2 holds two distinct cruxes and can be French-freed at 5.10a for parties not wanting to commit to the full 5.11a; slab sections give way to steep, balancy overlap moves. A belay bolt marks the route's start on a small ledge.

Ascends the south face starting in a small left-facing bolted dihedral; a highlight is a 5.11- slab traverse around pitch 5. Rated 3.8/5 by climbers with 182+ votes, considered a quality alpine trad testpiece alongside the neighboring Passenger and South Arete.
Do not underestimate The Horn as a simple scramble: despite the modest 5.5 grade, the final summit pitch is run-out and the rock demands careful gear placement.

moves.value: From Flapjack Lakes, leave the Gladys Divide trail at about 4,400 ft, short of the divide near a small pond, and climb an open snow and rock slope southeast toward Sawtooth Pass. Snow lingers on it into midsummer, so carry an axe early in the season. Below the pass, traverse right on loose, exposed class 3-4 ground under the west face of The Fin to the notch south of The Horn.
moves.from: Above Flapjack Lakes, the standard approach leaves the Gladys Divide trail at about 4,400 ft, short of the divide near a small pond, and climbs an open snow/rock slope southeast toward Sawtooth Pass - snow lingers on it into midsummer, so carry an axe early in the season. Below the pass, traverse right on loose, exposed class 3-4 ground under the west face of The Fin to the notch south of The Horn.

beta_new: Shares its start with The Tiger before splitting into its own line. Quality 5.10 climbing (some sections still lichen-flecked) is interspersed with harder cruxes on immaculate rock; treat the grades as provisional, since the route has seen very few repeats. The original 1969 aid ascent was protected almost entirely by pitons, plus 1 bolt; the free ascent added 3 protection bolts (with FA-party Jim Langdon's permission) on sections that had been aided via upward-driven knifeblade pitons.
A crux start on below-average rock quality for Keechelus, then the route is basically over. Also toprope-able by walking up.

moves.from: , but the anchor ledge is slanting and dirty — use a personal anchor system (PAS) when clipping in

beta_new: Follow the standard Snowfield Peak approach via Pyramid Lake to reach the Colonial-Neve col (approximately 6,800-6,900 feet). Traverse westward along the Neve Glacier staying near the glacier edge to avoid steep snow. Pass Horseman's Pack (8,156 ft) and The Horseman (7,760 ft), then turn north following the glacier edge to the southeast ridge of The Needle. Ascend the snow arete, bypassing the bergshrund, to gain the rocky ridge. Climb sustained Class 3 scrambling with full exposure, turning west around a corner. The final knife-edge ridge section before the summit can be crossed straddled (à cheval) or via an awkward mantle traverse. Exposed moves throughout.

A 'choose-your-own-adventure' wall route: the topo describes a default line but notes several parallel options at P1, P3 and P4. Rock is generally solid but still lichen-covered and loose in spots since the routes are relatively young (established 2007+). No bolts and very little fixed gear - tree slings mark some anchors, including a memorable 'spiral tree' landmark on P3.

Known only from Wayne Wallace, Colin Haley (age 17), and Mark Bunker's four-day, 14-summit Southern Pickets Enchainment (July 2003), where Pyramid was climbed via its east ridge/face at II 5.8 immediately after Inspiration Peak and before Mt. Degenhardt. It is not established as a stand-alone objective, so no dedicated approach or descent for climbing this line on its own is known — parties would likely use the same general approach as the South Route (Terror Basin/Crescent Creek Basin via the Barrier crossing), but that connection is an assumption, not confirmed.

From a high camp near the Terror Glacier or in Crescent Creek Basin, parties cross The Barrier (the connecting ridge between Terror and Crescent Creek basins) and work across broken, sometimes loose terrain toward the notch south of Mount Degenhardt, then traverse east along the connecting ridge onto Pyramid's west side. The line climbs a gully/couloir system on scrambling terrain with a few low fifth-class moves; staying left in the gully rather than attempting the overhanging rock directly above it is reported as the easier, more sensible line. Rock quality is inconsistent — solid gneiss in places, dirt- and choss-covered in others — and the peak sees comparatively little independent traffic, most parties tagging it en route between Degenhardt and Inspiration Peak.

The East Ridge route involves vertical to overhanging rock on pitons to avoid a loose gully below, followed by approximately half a mile of alpine ridge climbing. The route was established as a first ascent during the Complete Southern Pickets Traverse in July 2003.

moves.value: The base is reached by a snow and scree approach from the Mount Terror/Rake notch.
moves.from: Access is gained via a snow and scree approach from the Mount Terror/Rake notch.

beta_new: P1 (5.9, ~100 ft): bouldery move off the ground to easier terrain, belay below a small rotting tree. P2 (5.10a, ~100 ft): move into a groove, tough moves out right where climbing eases. P3 (5.10a, ~100 ft): fun climbing into a dihedral crux, short slab to 'Launch Ledge'; move the belay left ~30 ft before P4. P4 (5.11c, ~195 ft, 'The Scoop'): nice crack into a corner, sustained finger/hand jams up and left, finishing with a 5.10 hand crack to a nice belay ledge (a 5.10+ variation, 'Nectar', skips the crux via a hand crack to the right). P5 (5.10b, ~100 ft): down and left on a small ledge into a slab dihedral (small cams/nuts useful, wet early season), out left of a roof to a belay ledge. P6 (5.10a, ~100 ft): right side up, back left to a rock tooth, a nice 5.9 dihedral to a small roof and final ledge (tree belay). P7-10: easy fifth-class climbing up and left to the summit and the balanced rock.

P1: cracks and a corner past a small tree, up right to a ledge below an obvious roof (5.10d). P2: finger crack to the roof, out the crack, turn the lip and 12 more feet to a belay ledge — multiple #2 cams needed (C1 or 5.12d). P3: right on flakes and knobs into a wonderful dihedral (5.9+). P4: easier ground on runout chickenheads to a treed ledge (5.7). P5: up the corner over the pillar top, right and into a cave/alcove (5.10). P6/7: splitter cracks up the headwall (5.11a) through a flaring slot into a 0.75" left-facing corner, delicate stemming to a good ledge. P8: short chimney back left to a better ledge (5.8). P9+: simul-climb blocky ground to the summit boulder problem.

Parties approach via the Snow Lakes Trail into the Core Enchantments basin, then leave the trail to ascend talus and granite buttresses on Temple's south side. The line climbs mostly class 3-4 terrain - slabs, ledges, and blocky ribs - with exposure increasing near the top, finishing with a short low-5th-class (5.3-5.6) section through a ramp/notch onto the small, airy summit. A helmet and a light rack are commonly carried for the final moves.

moves.from: ; most parties descend by rappelling and downclimbing the route

beta_new: Technical, slabby corners low on the route give way to steep, physical, and strenuous climbing higher up. All but one of the 11 pitches is rated 5.10 or harder, with a bouldery 5.12b crux (underclings under a roof) at pitch 7. Well-placed bolts protect the hardest moves, but some 5.11- sections require finicky natural gear.

From the gully scramble (as per West Face), from the sandy ledge climb 10 ft of 5.7 and step left to a small ledge below a left-facing corner with a bolt about 8 ft up. P1 (20m, 5.11, 1 bolt): the corner to a 2-bolt ledge belay. P2 (20m, 5.11, 5 bolts): traverse left past bolts and knobs, layback past 3 bolts to a 2-bolt belay. P3 (40m, 5.11+, 3 bolts): up a seam, an insecure crux to the 'flower power' crack, then a steeper corner to the 'Sky Lounge' ledge (2 bolts). P4 (45m, 5.12, 8 bolts): traverse right, up a featured slab (5.10), through a power flare on tips-to-fingers crack to a roof, traverse left under the roof, stem past a bolt (avoiding a big flake) to a 2-bolt anchor in an alcove — the last rappel point on the route. P5 (30m, 5.11-, no bolts): small roof to a long hand/finger crack, trending right to a sandy alcove belay (shared with Let It Burn's P6/7 stance). P6+: finishes per Let It Burn to the summit.

Pitch 1 (5.10-, 6 bolts + gear to a chain anchor): a thin corner crack (~5.8) on small cams leads to low-fifth climbing before the first bolt at ~35 ft, then mixed bolts/gear to a large ledge, then short 5.10 climbing to anchors. Pitch 2 (5.10, 7 bolts to a 2-bolt anchor): bolts traverse right; well-bolted and takes no gear, but somewhat loose and dirty as of 2025, with one bolt hidden until higher and the climber going out of the belayer's sight.

moves.from: Pitch 1 (5.10-, 6 bolts + gear to a chain anchor)

beta_new: Six bolted pitches of clean, well-protected face and corner climbing (5.7, 5.8+, 5.7, 5.8, 5.9+ crux, 5.6) followed by an unroped scramble to the summit; established in 2019 as a fully bolted alternative to the trad South Face and Southwest Face lines, and a good option when those are congested.

Five pitches of bolted face/corner climbing (5.8-5.10b) starting left of a large gully west of The Tooth Fairy, crux on the technical 4th pitch's v-slot, followed by roughly 100m of unprotected 3rd/4th-class scrambling up the North Ridge to the true summit.

From the Hidden Lake Trail, leave the maintained tread to gain a heather-covered ridge, cross a small unnamed glacier on the peak's north side, and descend a steep, loose gully nicknamed the 'Drainage of Despair' to reach the base of the East Ridge. Climb ramps and a slabby section up and right to the ridge crest (an old rappel anchor marks easier ground above), then a short, exposed low-5th-class pinnacle pitch with sparse protection gains the true summit. The technical crux is a committing 4th-class move used to gain the ridge itself from a ledge system below.
